title: Keep Distributed Training Running with Automated Workload Recovery | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA open-sourced NVIDIA Recovery, a cluster-level service in its DSX OS stack that automatically detects, attributes, isolates and restarts failed distributed training jobs. The case rests on compounding failure math (a 10,000-GPU job has ~0.005% odds of a clean day) and production data showing ~8,550 anomalies over three months on one cluster with 69s/94s mean detection/action latency.

insights.claim: If each GPU has a 99.9% chance of running a day without failure, a job spanning 10,000 GPUs has only about a 0.005% chance of completing that day uninterrupted, so failures are a near-certainty for frontier-scale training.
insights.speaker: Ripple Patel
insights.so_what: Reliability, not just raw GPU count, bounds the effective compute of large training clusters; resilience software becomes a value lever.
insights.quote: At cluster scale, rare per-GPU failures compound.

insights.claim: In an 11-month study of 24,000 A100 GPUs at Meta, hardware failures interrupted fewer than 1% of jobs, yet those jobs accounted for 19% of GPU runtime, because the largest, longest-running jobs are the most exposed.
insights.speaker: Ripple Patel
insights.so_what: Failure cost is concentrated in the biggest jobs, so losses scale disproportionately as model training runs grow.
insights.quote: hardware failures interrupted fewer than 1% of jobs while those jobs accounted for 19% of GPU runtime

insights.claim: Manual recovery of distributed training becomes unsustainable at scale because each interruption requires log analysis, fault isolation and checkpoint restart while affected GPUs sit idle, and overlapping failures compound engineering burden and wasted GPU-hours.
insights.speaker: Ripple Patel
insights.so_what: Idle GPU-hours during recovery directly inflate training cost and time-to-train, creating demand for automation in the AI operations stack.
insights.quote: Manual recovery becomes unsustainable when it must cover every training job across a cluster, around the clock, at scale.

insights.claim: NVIDIA frames training efficiency in terms of goodput: the cumulative impact of disruptions and recovery overhead determines how efficiently wall-clock time converts into productive training progress.
insights.speaker: Ripple Patel
insights.so_what: Goodput is the operative metric for AI factory ROI, shifting competition toward utilization and uptime software, not just hardware specs.

insights.claim: From July 9 to Oct. 9, NVIDIA Recovery monitoring on one training cluster covered nearly 200 jobs per day and recorded about 8,550 anomaly detections, with mean detection latency of 69 seconds and mean recovery-action latency of 94 seconds.
insights.speaker: Ripple Patel
insights.so_what: Roughly 90+ anomalies per day on one cluster quantifies how frequent interruptions are and how much time automation can reclaim.
insights.quote: mean detection and recovery-action latencies of 69 and 94 seconds, respectively
insights.locator: Our production observations underscore the need

insights.claim: The authors caveat that recovery-action latency ends at the automated action, and scheduling plus checkpoint restoration still determine when productive training actually resumes.
insights.speaker: Ripple Patel
insights.so_what: Headline latency figures understate total downtime; checkpointing speed and scheduling remain bottlenecks and adjacent opportunities.
insights.quote: Recovery-action latency ends at the automated action; scheduling and checkpoint restoration determine when productive training resumes.
insights.locator: Our production observations underscore the need

insights.claim: NVIDIA Recovery's architect says it is integrated into NVIDIA Mission Control and DGX Cloud and used across NVIDIA's fleet of more than 100,000 GPUs.
insights.speaker: Ripple Patel
insights.so_what: Indicates NVIDIA's own internal fleet scale and that the tool is battle-tested before being open-sourced to customers.
insights.quote: used across NVIDIA’s fleet of more than 100,000 GPUs

insights.claim: IBM Research ran NVIDIA Recovery in monitor mode on its Slurm cluster, compared its advice with manual decisions, then enabled autonomous action and is now refining failure patterns with NVIDIA.
insights.speaker: Ripple Patel
insights.so_what: Early enterprise/research adoption signals traction for NVIDIA's software layer beyond its own fleet.
insights.quote: They ran in monitor mode first, compared the advice with their own manual recovery decisions, and enabled autonomous action after validating the signal.

insights.claim: Verda, described as a neocloud and the first NVIDIA Cloud Partner to deploy NVIDIA Recovery, runs it on VictoriaLogs instead of Loki and has contributed a connector and pull requests, kicking off the OSS partner program.
insights.speaker: Ripple Patel
insights.so_what: Neoclouds adopting NVIDIA's ops software deepens ecosystem lock-in around NVIDIA's AI factory stack.
insights.quote: Verda, the first NVIDIA Cloud Partner to deploy it, runs NVIDIA Recovery with VictoriaLogs and has submitted its first pull requests.
insights.locator: IBM Research has deployed NVIDIA Recovery

insights.claim: NVIDIA positions workload recovery as a distinct cluster-level coordination problem separate from break-fix hardware automation, in-job libraries like NVRx, and workload managers like Slurm.
insights.speaker: Ripple Patel
insights.so_what: NVIDIA is carving out and filling a new software layer in AI infrastructure operations, expanding its stack beyond chips.
insights.quote: Workload recovery is a distinct coordination problem
insights.locator: Workload recovery is a distinct coordination problem

insights.claim: NVIDIA Recovery is part of DSX OS, NVIDIA's open-source, Apache 2.0-licensed modular software portfolio for AI factory operations within the DSX AI Factory Platform, alongside components like NVSentinel, NVRx and NVIDIA Attribution.
insights.speaker: Ripple Patel
insights.so_what: Open-sourcing an AI-factory operating layer is a platform play that raises switching costs for NVIDIA hardware buyers.
insights.quote: NVIDIA Recovery is part of DSX OS, NVIDIA’s open-source software layer for AI factory operations.
insights.locator: NVIDIA Recovery is part of DSX OS

insights.claim: The resilience layers are designed without hard dependencies so customers can adopt individual components or plug in their own, including their own attribution service.
insights.speaker: Ripple Patel
insights.so_what: Modularity lowers adoption friction, a deliberate tactic to spread NVIDIA software into heterogeneous existing clusters.
insights.quote: These layers operate independently without hard dependencies

insights.claim: NVIDIA Recovery runs a four-stage loop of detect, attribute, isolate and restart-or-stop, recognizing PyTorch, NCCL, CUDA and interconnect failure patterns and flagging stragglers by sustained throughput degradation versus a recent baseline.
insights.speaker: Ripple Patel
insights.so_what: Shows the failure taxonomy that matters in production training, informing where reliability spend goes.

insights.claim: New deployments default to monitor mode, publishing recommendations without scheduler actions, so operators can validate signal-to-noise before enabling autonomous recovery.
insights.speaker: Ripple Patel
insights.so_what: Trust-building rollout design suggests operators remain cautious about autonomous control of expensive GPU jobs.
insights.quote: New deployments start in monitor mode by default.
insights.locator: Running it: Monitor mode and the audit trail

insights.claim: NVIDIA Recovery currently supports Slurm (including Slurm on Kubernetes via slurm-operator), with Slurm job-array recovery and native Kubernetes recovery starting with JobSet and Kubeflow PyTorchJob coming next.
insights.speaker: Ripple Patel
insights.so_what: Kubernetes support would extend the tool to cloud-native AI platforms, broadening NVIDIA's software reach.
